## Introduction

This article introduces grouped random effects in `stLMM` through simulated
Gaussian models and matched `lme4` fits. We progress from random intercepts to
independent and correlated slopes, crossed groups, and nested groups with shared
or parent-specific variances. Each example compares known generating values
with estimated parameters or group coefficients.

The main examples use the default separate IID sampler. After the model
examples, we examine combined fixed-plus-group coefficients and compare separate
and collapsed IID sampling. [An optional appendix](#additional-comparisons)
contains detailed diagnostics, timings, and binomial and count comparisons.

### Model choices and formula alignment

Three choices describe a grouped model [@BatesMaechlerBolkerWalker2015lme4]:

- **Coefficients:** which intercepts or slopes vary among groups.
- **Grouping:** one factor, crossed factors, or nested factors. A child is
  nested when it belongs to exactly one parent. Crossed factors are not nested
  within one another, as when observers visit several sites and sites have
  several observers.
- **Covariance:** whether coefficients within a group are independent or
  correlated, and whether groups share the same covariance matrix.

Groups remain independent of one another in a correlated `iid()` term;
correlation refers to its intercept and slope departures within each group.
Nesting describes membership, while `by` allows a separate child-effect
variance or covariance for each parent.

Every row below includes the same fixed part, `y ~ x`. Here `x` is numeric.
The entries show the random-effect terms to add.

| Structure | stLMM | lme4 |
|:--|:--|:--|
| One random intercept | `iid(group)` | <code>(1 &#124; group)</code> |
| Independent intercept and slope, separate | `iid(group) + iid(group):x` | <code>(1 &#124; group) + (0 + x &#124; group)</code> |
| Independent intercept and slope, compact | `iid(group, ~ 1 + x, cov_model = "independent")` | <code>(1 + x &#124;&#124; group)</code> |
| Correlated intercept and slope | `iid(group, ~ 1 + x)` | <code>(1 + x &#124; group)</code> |
| Crossed site and observer intercepts | `iid(site) + iid(observer)` | <code>(1 &#124; site) + (1 &#124; observer)</code> |
| Plots nested in stands, shared plot variance | `iid(stand) + iid(stand_plot)` | <code>(1 &#124; stand) + (1 &#124; stand_plot)</code> |
| Plots nested in stands, variance by stand | `iid(stand) + iid(plot, by = stand)` | Separate indicator-weighted plot terms; see the `by` example. |

For the nested model with a shared child variance, create a globally unique
child identifier first:

```r
dat$stand_plot <- interaction(dat$stand, dat$plot, drop = TRUE)
```

The matching `lme4` shorthand is `(1 | stand/plot)`, which expands to parent
and parent–child intercept terms. Plot labels such as `p01` can repeat across
stands, but `iid(plot)` alone would treat all occurrences of `p01` as the same
group. `by = stand` distinguishes the nested parent–plot pairs internally
and estimates separate plot-effect variance parameters for each stand.

With matching variance priors, the two independent coefficient forms use the same
scalar sampler. The correlated form uses an IW covariance prior. Covariates
enter on the supplied scale; the user chooses their centering and scaling.
The [getting-started article](v01-getting-started.html#grouped-random-effects)
describes prior syntax and prediction to new groups.

### Reading the results

`stLMM` reports posterior means and central 95% credible intervals under the
specified priors. `lme4` supplies REML point estimates for the Gaussian models.
The methods therefore need not give identical estimates. A single simulated
dataset also need not yield intervals containing every generating value.

Gaussian tables report **variances**, not standard deviations. The recovery
plots show known group coefficients against their estimates, with `stLMM`
credible intervals and `lme4` point estimates. Diagnostics use three chains and
rank-normalized R-hat, bulk ESS, and tail ESS from the optional `posterior`
package [@Vehtari2021Rhat]. Full diagnostic tables are in the appendix.

```{r helpers}
#| include: false
format_interval <- function(mean, lower, upper){
  sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", mean, lower, upper)
}
round_numeric_columns <- function(x, digits = 3){
  is_num <- vapply(x, is.numeric, logical(1))
  x[is_num] <- lapply(x[is_num], round, digits = digits)
  x
}
posterior_means <- function(fit, burn = 500L){
  draws <- as_samples(fit, burn = burn, metadata = FALSE)
  vapply(draws, mean, numeric(1))
}
diagnostic_table <- function(fit, parameters, burn = 500L){
  out <- summary(fit, burn = burn, diagnostic_method = "rank")
  out$diagnostics[parameters, c("parameter", "rhat", "ess_bulk", "ess_tail"),
                  drop = FALSE]
}
parameter_recovery_table <- function(fit, truth, reml, burn = gaussian_burn){
  out <- summary(fit, parameters = names(truth), burn = burn,
                 diagnostic_method = "rank")
  data.frame(parameter = names(truth), truth = unname(truth),
    out$parameters[, c("mean", "q2.5", "q97.5")],
    lme4 = unname(reml[names(truth)]),
    out$diagnostics[, c("rhat", "ess_bulk", "ess_tail")], row.names = NULL)
}
show_estimates <- function(tab, labels = tab$parameter){
  knitr::kable(data.frame(Quantity = labels, Simulated = round(tab$truth, 3),
    stLMM = format_interval(tab$mean, tab$q2.5, tab$q97.5),
    lme4 = round(tab$lme4, 3)), row.names = FALSE,
    caption = "stLMM posterior mean [95% credible interval] and lme4 estimate")
}
coefficient_recovery_table <- function(combined, truth, reml){
  data.frame(truth = unname(truth),
    combined$parameters[, c("mean", "q2.5", "q97.5")], lme4 = unname(reml),
    combined$diagnostics[, c("rhat", "ess_bulk", "ess_tail")], row.names = NULL)
}
group_coefficient_recovery <- function(combined, dat, fit){
  info <- combined$quantities
  truth <- attr(dat, "true_coefficients")
  reml <- as.matrix(coef(fit)$group)
  tab <- coefficient_recovery_table(combined,
    truth[cbind(match(info$group_group, rownames(truth)),
                match(info$coefficient, colnames(truth)))],
    reml[cbind(match(info$group_group, rownames(reml)),
               match(info$coefficient, colnames(reml)))])
  tab$coefficient <- info$coefficient
  tab
}
plot_coefficient_recovery <- function(tab){
  p <- ggplot(tab, aes(x = truth)) +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "grey45", linewidth = 0.4) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = q2.5, ymax = q97.5), width = 0,
                  color = stlmm_color("primary"), alpha = 0.3) +
    geom_point(aes(y = mean, color = "stLMM"), size = 1.5) +
    geom_point(aes(y = lme4, color = "lme4"), shape = 4, size = 1.5) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(stLMM = stlmm_color("primary"),
                                  lme4 = stlmm_color("secondary"))) +
    labs(x = "Simulated combined coefficient", y = "Estimated combined coefficient",
         color = "Estimate") + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
  if("coefficient" %in% names(tab))
    p <- p + facet_wrap(~ coefficient, scales = "free", labeller = as_labeller(
      c("(Intercept)" = "Intercept", x = "Slope for x")))
  p
}
fixed_effect_table <- function(fit, lme4_fit, truth, burn = 500L){
  draws <- as_samples(fit, burn = burn, metadata = FALSE)[names(truth)]
  data.frame(Quantity = names(truth), Simulated = unname(truth),
    stLMM = format_interval(vapply(draws, mean, numeric(1)),
      vapply(draws, quantile, numeric(1), 0.025),
      vapply(draws, quantile, numeric(1), 0.975)),
    lme4 = round(unname(fixef(lme4_fit)[names(truth)]), 3))
}
sd_comparison <- function(fit, lme4_fit, truth, burn){
  sd_draws <- sqrt(as_samples(fit, burn = burn)[["iid_1_sigma_sq"]])
  data.frame(Quantity = "Group standard deviation", Simulated = truth,
    stLMM = format_interval(mean(sd_draws), quantile(sd_draws, 0.025),
                            quantile(sd_draws, 0.975)),
    lme4 = round(attr(VarCorr(lme4_fit)$group, "stddev")[[1]], 3))
}
iid_random_effect_compare <- function(st_fit, lme4_fit, st_term = 1L,
                                      lme4_column = "(Intercept)",
                                      burn = 500L){
  st_mean <- posterior_means(st_fit, burn = burn)
  prefix <- paste0("iid_", st_term, "_")
  st_re <- st_mean[grep(paste0("^", prefix), names(st_mean))]
  names(st_re) <- sub(paste0("^", prefix), "", names(st_re))

  lme4_re <- ranef(lme4_fit)$group[[lme4_column]]
  names(lme4_re) <- rownames(ranef(lme4_fit)$group)

  common <- intersect(names(st_re), names(lme4_re))
  data.frame(
    group = common,
    stLMM = unname(st_re[common]),
    lme4 = unname(lme4_re[common])
  )
}
```

## Gaussian grouped models {#gaussian-models}

All examples include a fixed intercept and slope for `x`. We use explicit IG
priors for scalar variances and an IW prior for a correlated coefficient vector.
The prior scales belong to the supplied data units; the package does not rescale
covariates automatically. Chain lengths vary because the models mix at different
rates; the appendix reports the retained draws and diagnostics.

### One grouping factor: random intercepts

Start with $y_{ig}=\beta_0+\beta_x x_{ig}+u_g+\epsilon_{ig}$, where
$u_g\sim N(0,\sigma_u^2)$ and $\epsilon_{ig}\sim N(0,\tau^2)$.
There are 50 groups and 12 observations per group. The population intercept
and slope are 1 and 0.8, the group standard deviation is 0.6, and the residual
standard deviation is 0.4.

```{r simulate-intercepts}
set.seed(101)
intercept_dat <- data.frame(
  group = factor(rep(sprintf("g%02d", 1:50), each = 12)),
  x = rep(seq(-1, 1, length.out = 12), 50)
)
intercept_u <- setNames(rnorm(50, sd = 0.6), levels(intercept_dat$group))
intercept_dat$y <- 1 + 0.8 * intercept_dat$x +
  intercept_u[intercept_dat$group] + rnorm(nrow(intercept_dat), sd = 0.4)
```

```{r fit-intercepts}
intercept_st_time <- system.time({
  intercept_st <- stLMM(
    y ~ x + iid(group), intercept_dat,
    priors = list(resid = list(tau_sq = ig(2, 0.5)),
                  iid_1 = list(sigma_sq = ig(2, 0.5))),
    n_samples = 16000, chains = 3, chain_control = list(seed = 101),
    verbose = FALSE
  )
})
intercept_lme4_time <- system.time({
  intercept_lme4 <- lmer(y ~ x + (1 | group), intercept_dat, REML = TRUE)
})
```

```{r intercept-recovery}
intercept_truth <- c("(Intercept)" = 1, x = 0.8, tau_sq = 0.4^2,
                     iid_1_sigma_sq = 0.6^2)
intercept_reml <- c(fixef(intercept_lme4), tau_sq = sigma(intercept_lme4)^2,
                    iid_1_sigma_sq = VarCorr(intercept_lme4)$group[1, 1])
intercept_parameters <- parameter_recovery_table(
  intercept_st, intercept_truth, intercept_reml)
show_estimates(intercept_parameters, c("Fixed intercept", "Fixed slope", "Residual variance", "Group variance"))

intercept_combined <- summary(intercept_st, type = "combined",
  coefficients = "(Intercept)", terms = "iid_1", burn = gaussian_burn,
  diagnostic_method = "rank")
intercept_groups <- intercept_combined$quantities$group_group
intercept_recovery <- coefficient_recovery_table(intercept_combined,
  1 + intercept_u[intercept_groups],
  coef(intercept_lme4)$group[intercept_groups, "(Intercept)"])
```

```{r intercept-recovery-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
plot_coefficient_recovery(intercept_recovery)
```

The plotted quantity is $\beta_0+u_g$, the group baseline at `x = 0`.
The [combined-coefficient lesson](#combined-coefficients) explains how its
interpretation and diagnostics differ from those of its two components.

### One grouping factor: independent intercepts and slopes

Now each group has an intercept departure and a slope departure, with zero
covariance between them. The two equivalent formula forms are listed above;
the fit below uses separate terms. We simulate 30 groups with 15 observations
per group, fixed coefficients 1 and 2, and residual and group standard deviations
all equal to 0.5.

```{r simulate-gaussian-small}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show simulation code"
simulate_gaussian_slope_data <- function(seed = 1,
                                         n_group = 30,
                                         n_per_group = 15,
                                         beta = c("(Intercept)" = 1, x = 2),
                                         sigma_intercept = 0.5,
                                         sigma_slope = 0.5,
                                         tau = 0.5,
                                         correlation = 0){
  set.seed(seed)

  group <- factor(rep(sprintf("g%02d", seq_len(n_group)),
                      each = n_per_group))
  x <- rep(seq(-1, 1, length.out = n_per_group), n_group) +
    rnorm(n_group * n_per_group, sd = 0.08)

  covariance <- matrix(c(
    sigma_intercept^2, correlation * sigma_intercept * sigma_slope,
    correlation * sigma_intercept * sigma_slope, sigma_slope^2
  ), 2, 2)
  alpha <- matrix(rnorm(2 * n_group), n_group, 2) %*% chol(covariance)
  alpha_intercept <- alpha[, 1]
  alpha_slope <- alpha[, 2]
  names(alpha_intercept) <- levels(group)
  names(alpha_slope) <- levels(group)

  mu <- beta[["(Intercept)"]] + beta[["x"]] * x +
    alpha_intercept[group] + alpha_slope[group] * x

  dat <- data.frame(
    y = mu + rnorm(length(mu), sd = tau),
    x = x,
    group = group
  )
  combined <- sweep(alpha, 2, beta, "+")
  dimnames(combined) <- list(levels(group), names(beta))
  attr(dat, "true_coefficients") <- combined
  dat
}

gauss_dat <- simulate_gaussian_slope_data(seed = 1)
gauss_true_beta <- c("(Intercept)" = 1, x = 2)
```

```{r fit-gaussian-small}
gauss_st_time <- system.time({
  gauss_st <- stLMM(
    y ~ x + iid(group) + x:iid(group),
    data = gauss_dat,
    priors = list(
      resid = list(tau_sq = ig(2, 0.5)),
      iid_1 = list(sigma_sq = ig(2, 0.5)),
      iid_2 = list(sigma_sq = ig(2, 0.5))
    ),
    n_samples = 16000,
    chains = 3,
    verbose = FALSE
  )
})

gauss_lme4_time <- system.time({
  gauss_lme4 <- lmer(
    y ~ x + (1 | group) + (0 + x | group),
    data = gauss_dat,
    REML = TRUE
  )
})
```

```{r gaussian-independent-results}
gauss_truth <- c(gauss_true_beta, tau_sq = 0.25,
  iid_1_sigma_sq = 0.25, iid_2_sigma_sq = 0.25)
gauss_vc <- VarCorr(gauss_lme4)
gauss_variances <- setNames(vapply(gauss_vc, function(v) v[1, 1], numeric(1)),
  vapply(gauss_vc, function(v) colnames(v)[1], character(1)))
gauss_reml <- c(fixef(gauss_lme4), tau_sq = sigma(gauss_lme4)^2,
  iid_1_sigma_sq = unname(gauss_variances["(Intercept)"]),
  iid_2_sigma_sq = unname(gauss_variances["x"]))
gauss_parameters <- parameter_recovery_table(gauss_st, gauss_truth, gauss_reml)
show_estimates(gauss_parameters, c("Fixed intercept", "Fixed slope",
  "Residual variance", "Intercept variance", "Slope variance"))
gauss_combined <- summary(gauss_st, type = "combined",
  coefficients = c("(Intercept)", "x"), terms = c("iid_1", "iid_2"),
  burn = gaussian_burn, diagnostic_method = "rank")
gauss_recovery <- group_coefficient_recovery(gauss_combined, gauss_dat, gauss_lme4)
```

```{r gaussian-independent-recovery-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
plot_coefficient_recovery(gauss_recovery)
```

### One grouping factor: correlated intercepts and slopes

The compact formula `iid(group, ~ 1 + x)` estimates the covariance between a
group's intercept and slope departures:

$$
y_{ig}=(\beta_0+u_{0g})+(\beta_x+u_{xg})x_{ig}+\epsilon_{ig},\qquad
\begin{pmatrix}u_{0g}\\u_{xg}\end{pmatrix}\sim N_2(\mathbf{0},\Sigma),
\qquad \epsilon_{ig}\sim N(0,\tau^2).
$$

We simulate 60 groups with 12 observations each, group standard deviations 0.5,
and correlation 0.6. The variances are therefore 0.25 and the covariance is 0.15.
The residual standard deviation is also 0.5.

The IW prior below has dimension two, degrees of freedom 4, and mean
`diag(c(0.25, 0.25))`. It is a regularizing prior, not a noninformative choice.
The default separate sampler uses a conjugate IW covariance update.

```{r fit-gaussian-correlated}
gauss_cor_dat <- simulate_gaussian_slope_data(
  seed = 17, n_group = 60, n_per_group = 12, correlation = 0.6
)
cor_priors <- list(
  resid = list(tau_sq = ig(2, 0.5)),
  iid_1 = list(covariance = iw(df = 4, scale = diag(c(0.25, 0.25))))
)
cor_burn <- 2000L
gauss_cor_st_time <- system.time({
  gauss_cor_st <- stLMM(
    y ~ x + iid(group, ~ 1 + x), data = gauss_cor_dat,
    priors = cor_priors, collapse_iid = FALSE,
    n_samples = 8000, chains = 3,
    chain_control = list(seed = 17), verbose = FALSE
  )
})
gauss_cor_lme4_time <- system.time({
  gauss_cor_lme4 <- lmer(y ~ x + (1 + x | group), gauss_cor_dat, REML = TRUE)
})
```

```{r gaussian-correlated-results}
cor_truth <- c(gauss_true_beta, tau_sq = 0.25,
  "iid_1_cov[(Intercept),(Intercept)]" = 0.25,
  "iid_1_cov[x,(Intercept)]" = 0.15, "iid_1_cov[x,x]" = 0.25)
lme4_cov <- as.matrix(VarCorr(gauss_cor_lme4)$group)
cor_reml <- c(fixef(gauss_cor_lme4), tau_sq = sigma(gauss_cor_lme4)^2,
  "iid_1_cov[(Intercept),(Intercept)]" = lme4_cov[1, 1],
  "iid_1_cov[x,(Intercept)]" = lme4_cov[2, 1], "iid_1_cov[x,x]" = lme4_cov[2, 2])
cor_parameters <- parameter_recovery_table(gauss_cor_st, cor_truth, cor_reml,
                                          burn = cor_burn)
show_estimates(cor_parameters, c("Fixed intercept", "Fixed slope", "Residual variance",
  "Intercept variance", "Intercept–slope covariance", "Slope variance"))
```

The [sampler comparison](#iid-sampling-strategies) revisits this dataset and
plots recovered group intercepts and slopes under both sampling strategies.

### Crossed grouping factors

Suppose every one of 15 observers measures at each of 20 sites, twice per
site–observer pair. A site effect is shared by all observers at that site;
an observer effect is shared across the sites that observer visits. Neither
factor is nested within the other. The model is

$$
y_{iso}=\beta_0+\beta_x x_{iso}+u_s+v_o+\epsilon_{iso},
\qquad u_s\sim N(0,\sigma_s^2),\quad v_o\sim N(0,\sigma_o^2).
$$

The separate site and observer terms are independent. There is no additional
site–observer interaction effect in this model.

```{r simulate-crossed}
set.seed(103)
crossed_dat <- expand.grid(
  replicate = 1:2, site = sprintf("s%02d", 1:20),
  observer = sprintf("o%02d", 1:15), KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE
)
crossed_dat$site <- factor(crossed_dat$site)
crossed_dat$observer <- factor(crossed_dat$observer)
crossed_dat$x <- rep(c(-1, 1), 20 * 15)
site_u <- setNames(rnorm(20, sd = 0.6), levels(crossed_dat$site))
observer_v <- setNames(rnorm(15, sd = 0.35), levels(crossed_dat$observer))
crossed_dat$y <- 1 + 0.8 * crossed_dat$x + site_u[crossed_dat$site] +
  observer_v[crossed_dat$observer] + rnorm(nrow(crossed_dat), sd = 0.4)
```

```{r fit-crossed}
crossed_st_time <- system.time({
  crossed_st <- stLMM(
    y ~ x + iid(site) + iid(observer), crossed_dat,
    priors = list(resid = list(tau_sq = ig(2, 0.5)),
                  iid_1 = list(sigma_sq = ig(2, 0.5)),
                  iid_2 = list(sigma_sq = ig(2, 0.5))),
    n_samples = 40000, chains = 3, chain_control = list(seed = 103),
    verbose = FALSE
  )
})
crossed_lme4_time <- system.time({
  crossed_lme4 <- lmer(y ~ x + (1 | site) + (1 | observer),
                       crossed_dat, REML = TRUE)
})
```

```{r crossed-recovery}
crossed_truth <- c("(Intercept)" = 1, x = 0.8, tau_sq = 0.4^2,
                   iid_1_sigma_sq = 0.6^2, iid_2_sigma_sq = 0.35^2)
crossed_reml <- c(fixef(crossed_lme4), tau_sq = sigma(crossed_lme4)^2,
                  iid_1_sigma_sq = VarCorr(crossed_lme4)$site[1, 1],
                  iid_2_sigma_sq = VarCorr(crossed_lme4)$observer[1, 1])
crossed_parameters <- parameter_recovery_table(
  crossed_st, crossed_truth, crossed_reml)
show_estimates(crossed_parameters, c("Fixed intercept", "Fixed slope", "Residual variance", "Site variance", "Observer variance"))

crossed_combined <- summary(crossed_st, type = "combined",
  coefficients = "(Intercept)", terms = c("iid_1", "iid_2"),
  burn = gaussian_burn, diagnostic_method = "rank")
crossed_pairs <- data.frame(
  site = crossed_combined$quantities$group_site,
  observer = crossed_combined$quantities$group_observer, x = 0)
crossed_recovery <- coefficient_recovery_table(crossed_combined,
  1 + site_u[crossed_pairs$site] + observer_v[crossed_pairs$observer],
  predict(crossed_lme4, newdata = crossed_pairs))
```

```{r crossed-recovery-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
plot_coefficient_recovery(crossed_recovery)
```

Each point is a represented site's baseline for one observer,
$\beta_0+u_s+v_o$. In a partially crossed dataset, `summary(type = "combined")`
reports only represented combinations; it does not create every possible pair.

### Nested grouping factors with a shared child variance

Now observations belong to plots, and each physical plot belongs to one stand:

$$
y_{isp}=\beta_0+\beta_x x_{isp}+u_s+v_{sp}+\epsilon_{isp},
\qquad u_s\sim N(0,\sigma_s^2),\quad v_{sp}\sim N(0,\sigma_p^2).
$$

This nested model assumes a common plot-effect variance $\sigma_p^2$ across
stands. The example has 12 stands, 24 plots per stand, and six observations
per plot: 1,728 observations and 288 physical plots. Local plot labels repeat
across stands, so both fits below use a unique `stand_plot` identifier.

```{r simulate-nested}
#| code-summary: "Show nested simulation, retaining the generating effects"
simulate_nested_intercepts <- function(seed, child_sd = 0.5){
  set.seed(seed)
  d <- expand.grid(observation = 1:6, plot = sprintf("p%02d", 1:24),
                   stand = sprintf("s%02d", 1:12), KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE)
  d$stand <- factor(d$stand)
  d$plot <- factor(d$plot)
  d$stand_plot <- interaction(d$stand, d$plot, drop = TRUE, lex.order = TRUE)
  d$x <- rep(seq(-1, 1, length.out = 6), 12 * 24)
  child_sd <- setNames(rep_len(child_sd, 12), levels(d$stand))
  stand_effect <- setNames(rnorm(12, sd = 0.6), levels(d$stand))
  plot_rows <- match(levels(d$stand_plot), as.character(d$stand_plot))
  plot_effect <- setNames(rnorm(12 * 24,
    sd = child_sd[as.character(d$stand[plot_rows])]), levels(d$stand_plot))
  d$y <- 1 + 0.8 * d$x + stand_effect[d$stand] +
    plot_effect[d$stand_plot] + rnorm(nrow(d), sd = 0.4)
  list(data = d, stand_effect = stand_effect, plot_effect = plot_effect,
       child_sd = child_sd)
}
nested_sim <- simulate_nested_intercepts(seed = 104)
nested_dat <- nested_sim$data
```

```{r fit-nested}
nested_st_time <- system.time({
  nested_st <- stLMM(
    y ~ x + iid(stand) + iid(stand_plot), nested_dat,
    priors = list(resid = list(tau_sq = ig(2, 0.5)),
                  iid_1 = list(sigma_sq = ig(2, 0.5)),
                  iid_2 = list(sigma_sq = ig(2, 0.5))),
    n_samples = 60000, chains = 3, chain_control = list(seed = 104),
    verbose = FALSE
  )
})
nested_lme4_time <- system.time({
  nested_lme4 <- lmer(y ~ x + (1 | stand) + (1 | stand_plot),
                      nested_dat, REML = TRUE)
})
```

```{r nested-recovery}
nested_truth <- c("(Intercept)" = 1, x = 0.8, tau_sq = 0.4^2,
                  iid_1_sigma_sq = 0.6^2, iid_2_sigma_sq = 0.5^2)
nested_reml <- c(fixef(nested_lme4), tau_sq = sigma(nested_lme4)^2,
                 iid_1_sigma_sq = VarCorr(nested_lme4)$stand[1, 1],
                 iid_2_sigma_sq = VarCorr(nested_lme4)$stand_plot[1, 1])
nested_parameters <- parameter_recovery_table(
  nested_st, nested_truth, nested_reml)
show_estimates(nested_parameters, c("Fixed intercept", "Fixed slope", "Residual variance", "Stand variance", "Plot variance"))

nested_combined <- summary(nested_st, type = "combined",
  coefficients = "(Intercept)", terms = c("iid_1", "iid_2"),
  burn = gaussian_burn, diagnostic_method = "rank")
nested_pairs <- data.frame(stand = nested_combined$quantities$group_stand,
  stand_plot = nested_combined$quantities$group_stand_plot, x = 0)
nested_recovery <- coefficient_recovery_table(nested_combined,
  1 + nested_sim$stand_effect[nested_pairs$stand] +
    nested_sim$plot_effect[nested_pairs$stand_plot],
  predict(nested_lme4, newdata = nested_pairs))
```

```{r nested-recovery-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
plot_coefficient_recovery(nested_recovery)
```

The recovered baseline is $\beta_0+u_s+v_{sp}$. The stand effect is shared
by its plots; the plot effect is shared only by observations of that plot.

### Nested effects with parent-specific variances using by {#parent-specific-child-distributions-with-by}

Keep the same nesting, but now let the plot-effect variance differ by stand:

$$
v_{sp}\sim N(0,\sigma_{p,s}^2).
$$

`iid(plot, by = stand)` estimates these 12 variances. It does not add stand
intercepts automatically; `iid(stand)` supplies those. The same IG prior is
applied independently to each plot variance. These variances are neither
constrained equal nor linked by an estimated hyperprior.

```{r simulate-by}
by_sim <- simulate_nested_intercepts(seed = 105,
  child_sd = rep(c(0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1), 3))
by_dat <- by_sim$data
```

```{r fit-by-stlmm}
by_st_time <- system.time({
  by_st <- stLMM(
    y ~ x + iid(stand) + iid(plot, by = stand), by_dat,
    priors = list(resid = list(tau_sq = ig(2, 0.5)),
                  iid_1 = list(sigma_sq = ig(2, 0.5)),
                  iid_2 = list(sigma_sq = ig(2, 0.5))),
    n_samples = 160000, chains = 3, chain_control = list(seed = 105),
    verbose = FALSE
  )
})
```

For a matching `lme4` fit, create a numeric indicator for each stand and a
separate random coefficient for that indicator. For example,
`(0 + in_s01 | plot)` contributes only to observations in stand `s01`.
Separate terms have separate variances. Although plot labels repeat, their
coefficients belong to different terms, so plots in different stands do not
share an effect. The usual `(1 | stand/plot)` shorthand would impose a common
plot variance and would therefore fit a different model.

```{r fit-by-lme4}
by_stands <- levels(by_dat$stand)
by_indicators <- paste0("in_", by_stands)
for(i in seq_along(by_stands))
  by_dat[[by_indicators[i]]] <- as.numeric(by_dat$stand == by_stands[i])
by_formula <- as.formula(paste(
  "y ~ x + (1 | stand) +",
  paste0("(0 + ", by_indicators, " | plot)", collapse = " + ")
))
by_lme4_time <- system.time({
  by_lme4 <- lmer(by_formula, by_dat, REML = TRUE)
})
```

The comparison below matches variance components by indicator name rather
than their storage order. The `stLMM` output names identify the corresponding
stand explicitly.

```{r by-recovery}
by_variance_names <- paste0('iid_2[stand="', by_stands, '"]_sigma_sq')
by_truth <- c("(Intercept)" = 1, x = 0.8, tau_sq = 0.4^2,
              iid_1_sigma_sq = 0.6^2,
              setNames(unname(by_sim$child_sd^2), by_variance_names))
by_vc <- VarCorr(by_lme4)
by_reml <- c(fixef(by_lme4), tau_sq = sigma(by_lme4)^2,
             iid_1_sigma_sq = by_vc$stand[1, 1])
for(i in seq_along(by_indicators)){
  index <- which(vapply(by_vc, function(v)
    identical(colnames(v), by_indicators[i]), logical(1)))
  by_reml[by_variance_names[i]] <- by_vc[[index]][1, 1]
}
by_parameters <- parameter_recovery_table(by_st, by_truth, by_reml)
show_estimates(by_parameters[1:4, ], c("Fixed intercept", "Fixed slope",
  "Residual variance", "Stand variance"))
```

```{r by-variance-recovery-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
by_variances <- by_parameters[match(by_variance_names, by_parameters$parameter), ]
by_variances$stand <- factor(by_stands, levels = by_stands)
ggplot(by_variances, aes(stand)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = q2.5, ymax = q97.5), width = 0.15,
                color = stlmm_color("primary")) +
  geom_point(aes(y = mean, color = "stLMM"), size = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(y = lme4, color = "lme4"), shape = 4, size = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(y = truth, color = "Simulated"), shape = 18, size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(stLMM = stlmm_color("primary"),
    lme4 = stlmm_color("secondary"), Simulated = "grey20")) +
  labs(x = "Stand", y = "Plot-effect variance", color = "Value") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r by-combined-recovery}
by_combined <- summary(by_st, type = "combined",
  coefficients = "(Intercept)", terms = c("iid_1", "iid_2"),
  burn = gaussian_burn, diagnostic_method = "rank")
by_rows <- match(
  paste(by_combined$quantities$group_stand, by_combined$quantities$group_plot),
  paste(by_dat$stand, by_dat$plot))
by_pairs <- by_dat[by_rows, setdiff(names(by_dat), "y"), drop = FALSE]
by_pairs$x <- 0
by_recovery <- coefficient_recovery_table(by_combined,
  1 + by_sim$stand_effect[by_pairs$stand] +
    by_sim$plot_effect[by_pairs$stand_plot],
  predict(by_lme4, newdata = by_pairs))
```


Each stand's variance is informed by its 24 plot effects. Adding measurements
within those plots improves estimation of their effects, but does not create
more independent plots for estimating that variance. Compare uncertainty and
prior sensitivity accordingly.

For correlated child intercepts and slopes, use:

```r
y ~ x + iid(stand) + iid(plot, ~ 1 + x, by = stand)
```

That model has a separate IW covariance block for each stand; it does not
introduce covariance between different stands. Its `lme4` counterpart uses
one term such as `(0 + in_s01 + x_s01 | plot)` per stand, where
`x_s01 = x * in_s01`. The preceding executable example uses scalar plot effects.

For prediction, a new plot in a represented stand requires
`allow_new_levels = TRUE` and uses that stand's posterior child distribution.
A new stand is rejected even with that flag: the fitted model has no estimated
child distribution for it. These rules are described in the
[prediction reference](../reference/predict.stLMM_recovery.html).

## Combined coefficients and diagnostics {#combined-coefficients}

In the first example, $\beta_0$ is the center of the group-intercept distribution,
$u_g$ is a group departure, and $\beta_0+u_g$ is that group's baseline at `x = 0`.
The observations inform the sum directly. Fixed and group effects can compensate
for one another, so the sum can mix differently from its components.

`summary(type = "combined")` adds the coefficients within each iteration and
chain before computing intervals and diagnostics. It does not add separate
interval endpoints or combine separate R-hat values. The matching lme4 quantity
is `coef(fit)$group`; `ranef(fit)$group` returns only the group departures.

```{r gaussian-combined-summary}
intercept_combined <- summary(intercept_st, type = "combined",
  coefficients = "(Intercept)", terms = "iid_1", burn = gaussian_burn,
  diagnostic_method = "rank")
```

```{r gaussian-component-diagnostics}
#| code-summary: "Show separate and combined coefficient diagnostics"
trace_group <- levels(intercept_dat$group)[1]
component_summary <- summary(intercept_st,
  parameters = c("(Intercept)", paste0("iid_1_", trace_group)),
  burn = gaussian_burn, diagnostic_method = "rank")
group_row <- match(trace_group, intercept_combined$quantities$group_group)
component_parameters <- rbind(component_summary$parameters,
  intercept_combined$parameters[group_row, , drop = FALSE])
component_diagnostics <- rbind(component_summary$diagnostics,
  intercept_combined$diagnostics[group_row, , drop = FALSE])
knitr::kable(data.frame(Quantity = c("Fixed intercept", "Group departure",
  "Combined intercept"), stLMM = format_interval(component_parameters[, "mean"],
  component_parameters[, "q2.5"], component_parameters[, "q97.5"]),
  Rhat = round(component_diagnostics$rhat, 3),
  bulk_ESS = round(component_diagnostics$ess_bulk),
  tail_ESS = round(component_diagnostics$ess_tail)), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r gaussian-combined-traces, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
#| code-summary: "Show aligned-draw trace code"
trace_draws <- as_samples(intercept_st, burn = gaussian_burn)
trace_draws <- trace_draws[trace_draws$.iteration > max(trace_draws$.iteration) - 1500, ]
fixed_draws <- trace_draws[["(Intercept)"]]
group_draws <- trace_draws[[paste0("iid_1_", trace_group)]]
trace_labels <- c("Fixed intercept", "Group departure", "Combined intercept")
trace_data <- data.frame(iteration = rep(trace_draws$.iteration, 3),
  chain = factor(rep(trace_draws$.chain, 3)),
  quantity = factor(rep(trace_labels, each = nrow(trace_draws)), levels = trace_labels),
  value = c(fixed_draws, group_draws, fixed_draws + group_draws))
ggplot(trace_data, aes(iteration, value, color = chain)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.25, alpha = 0.65) +
  facet_wrap(~ quantity, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = stlmm_discrete_colors(3)) +
  labs(x = "Saved iteration", y = "Coefficient", color = "Chain") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The panels show the last 1,500 iterations of each chain on their own vertical
scales; the table uses all post-burn draws. Inspect the quantities you intend
to report, including the variance components. Good diagnostics for a sum do
not establish convergence of its components. R-hat near 1 (commonly below 1.01)
and adequate ESS are useful checks, alongside traces and Monte Carlo precision.
Increasing `burn` alone does not improve exploration.

The same approach applies to slopes and sums involving multiple IID terms.
Combined summaries concern coefficients before multiplication by covariates;
use `fitted()` or `predict()` for the complete predictor or response mean.

## Separate and collapsed IID sampling {#iid-sampling-strategies}

The correlated Gaussian model above can also be fit with `collapse_iid = TRUE`.
The default keeps IID coefficients separate and uses IW covariance draws;
collapsing integrates the coefficients out and uses Metropolis covariance updates.
For Gaussian models, `recover()` then draws the IID coefficients, jointly with
any structured effects. Call it before fitted values, prediction, or combined
coefficient summaries, including for IID-only fits.

Both strategies target the same posterior under the same priors. We use three
chains of 8,000 saved draws for each, discard the first 2,000, and use different
seeds. The lme4 comparison remains the same REML fit.

```{r fit-gaussian-collapsed}
gauss_cor_collapsed_time <- system.time({
  gauss_cor_collapsed <- stLMM(
    y ~ x + iid(group, ~ 1 + x), data = gauss_cor_dat,
    priors = cor_priors, collapse_iid = TRUE,
    n_samples = 8000, chains = 3,
    chain_control = list(seed = 117), verbose = FALSE
  )
})
set.seed(217)
gauss_cor_recovery_time <- system.time({
  gauss_cor_recovered <- recover(gauss_cor_collapsed,
    sub_sample = list(start = cor_burn + 1L))
})

cor_fits <- list(Separate = gauss_cor_st, Collapsed = gauss_cor_collapsed)
```

```{r gaussian-sampler-comparison}
cor_components <- lapply(cor_fits, function(fit){
  draws <- as_samples(fit, burn = cor_burn)
  vi <- draws[["iid_1_cov[(Intercept),(Intercept)]"]]
  vs <- draws[["iid_1_cov[x,x]"]]
  cv <- draws[["iid_1_cov[x,(Intercept)]"]]
  cbind(residual_variance = draws[["tau_sq"]], intercept_variance = vi,
        slope_variance = vs, intercept_slope_covariance = cv,
        correlation = cv / sqrt(vi * vs))
})
lme4_cov <- as.matrix(VarCorr(gauss_cor_lme4)$group)
cor_table <- data.frame(
  component = c("Residual variance", "Intercept variance", "Slope variance",
                "Intercept-slope covariance", "Correlation"),
  truth = c(0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.15, 0.6)
)
for(method in names(cor_components)){
  draws <- cor_components[[method]]
  cor_table[[method]] <- format_interval(colMeans(draws),
    apply(draws, 2, quantile, 0.025), apply(draws, 2, quantile, 0.975))
}
cor_table$lme4 <- c(sigma(gauss_cor_lme4)^2, diag(lme4_cov),
                    lme4_cov[1, 2], cov2cor(lme4_cov)[1, 2])

knitr::kable(round_numeric_columns(cor_table), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Posterior mean [95% credible interval] and lme4 REML estimate")
cor_parameter_names <- names(cor_truth)
cor_diagnostics <- lapply(cor_fits, function(fit)
  diagnostic_table(fit, cor_parameter_names, burn = cor_burn))
```

```{r gaussian-combined-diagnostics}
cor_coefficient_fits <- list(Separate = gauss_cor_st, Collapsed = gauss_cor_recovered)
cor_combined <- lapply(cor_coefficient_fits, function(fit)
  summary(fit, type = "combined", coefficients = c("(Intercept)", "x"),
          terms = "iid_1", burn = cor_burn, diagnostic_method = "rank"))
info <- cor_combined$Separate$quantities
cor_group_table <- data.frame(group = info$group_group, coefficient = info$coefficient)
index <- cbind(match(cor_group_table$group, levels(gauss_cor_dat$group)),
               match(cor_group_table$coefficient, c("(Intercept)", "x")))
cor_group_table$truth <- attr(gauss_cor_dat, "true_coefficients")[index]
cor_group_table$lme4 <- as.matrix(coef(gauss_cor_lme4)$group)[index]
cor_group_plot <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(cor_combined), function(method){
  p <- cor_combined[[method]]$parameters
  data.frame(cor_group_table, method = method, p[, c("mean", "q2.5", "q97.5")])
}))
```

The plot compares true group intercepts and slopes with the three estimates.
The two Bayesian intervals overlap closely; the separate and collapsed samples
come from independent MCMC runs. Agreement is assessed alongside the parameter
diagnostics, not from interval overlap alone.

```{r gaussian-correlated-group-comparison, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show three-way simulation-recovery plot"
ggplot(cor_group_plot, aes(truth, mean, color = method)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "grey45", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = q2.5, ymax = q97.5), width = 0,
                linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_point(size = 1.3, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = cor_group_table, aes(truth, lme4, color = "lme4"),
             inherit.aes = FALSE, shape = 4, size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Separate = stlmm_color("primary"),
    Collapsed = stlmm_color("accent"), lme4 = stlmm_color("secondary"))) +
  facet_wrap(~ coefficient, scales = "free", labeller = as_labeller(
    c("(Intercept)" = "Intercept", x = "Slope for x"))) +
  labs(x = "Simulated combined coefficient", y = "Estimated combined coefficient",
       color = "Method") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r gaussian-sampler-efficiency}
cor_fit_seconds <- c(Separate = gauss_cor_st_time[["elapsed"]],
                    Collapsed = gauss_cor_collapsed_time[["elapsed"]])
cor_recovery_seconds <- c(Separate = 0, Collapsed = gauss_cor_recovery_time[["elapsed"]])
cor_seconds <- cor_fit_seconds + cor_recovery_seconds
cor_efficiency <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(cor_fits), function(method){
  d <- cor_diagnostics[[method]]
  combined <- cor_combined[[method]]$diagnostics
  data.frame(Method = method, fit_seconds = cor_fit_seconds[[method]],
    recovery_seconds = cor_recovery_seconds[[method]],
    covariance_bulk_ESS_per_second = min(d$ess_bulk[-(1:2)]) / cor_seconds[[method]],
    combined_bulk_ESS_per_second = min(combined$ess_bulk) / cor_seconds[[method]])
}))
knitr::kable(round_numeric_columns(cor_efficiency), row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Sampler", "Fit (s)", "Recovery (s)",
    "Covariance min ESS/s", "Combined min ESS/s"))
```

The ESS rates use total fitting and recovery time, including discarded warmup
and burn-in. Each rate is the minimum bulk ESS within its set: residual/IID
covariance parameters, or all group intercepts and slopes. The REML fit takes
`r round(gauss_cor_lme4_time[["elapsed"]], 3)` seconds here; it does not produce
posterior samples or an MCMC ESS.

Coefficient and covariance efficiency can favor different strategies. These are
results for one dataset and machine. Joint collapsing is experimental, and IID
groups can increase factorization costs when combined with structured processes;
the [technical document](a12-modeling-software-details.html) explains the trade-offs.
The default remains `collapse_iid = FALSE`.

## Additional capabilities in lme4

The examples above cover shared capabilities. The following distinctions
help identify analyses that require a different interface or inferential
workflow from the one currently provided by `stLMM`.

| Capability | lme4 | Current stLMM interface |
|:--|:--|:--|
| General random-effect design formulas | Factor contrasts, interactions, and transformed predictors can enter random-effect design matrices through the formula. | IID coefficient formulas accept additive numeric variable names. Precompute additional numeric columns and grouping identifiers when needed. |
| More likelihood/link combinations | Native Poisson and Gamma GLMMs, and GLM links such as binomial complementary log-log, through `glmer()`. | Gaussian, binomial-logit, binomial-probit, and negative-binomial-log models. Poisson examples use an NB approximation. |
| Nonlinear mixed mean functions | `nlmer()` fits specified nonlinear mean functions with mixed effects. | The predictor is linear in its fixed and random coefficients. |
| Likelihood-based estimation and inference | ML/REML estimation, likelihood profiles, profile or bootstrap confidence intervals, and likelihood-based model comparisons. | Posterior simulation, prior specification, posterior intervals, and MCMC diagnostics. |
| Optimization and boundary diagnostics | Tools such as `isSingular()` inspect fitted covariance boundaries; optimizer controls address likelihood fitting. | Rank R-hat and ESS assess posterior simulation. They answer different questions from likelihood-boundary diagnostics. |

The [lmer](https://lme4.github.io/lme4/reference/lmer.html),
[glmer](https://lme4.github.io/lme4/reference/glmer.html), and
[nlmer](https://lme4.github.io/lme4/reference/nlmer.html) references describe
these interfaces. These distinctions concern supported specifications and
inferential methods, rather than a general ranking of the packages.

## Additional comparisons and diagnostics {#additional-comparisons}

These optional sections retain the full numerical diagnostics and the
non-Gaussian comparisons. The grouping syntax is unchanged across likelihoods;
see the [binomial](a08-binomial-models.html) and
[negative-binomial](a09-negative-binomial-counts.html) articles for fuller workflows.
For these GLMMs, `stLMM` uses posterior simulation, while the `lme4` calls below
use the Laplace likelihood approximation.

<details>
<summary>Gaussian parameter diagnostics and run lengths</summary>

The tables below retain diagnostics for individual parameters and combined
coefficients. Covariance and coefficient diagnostics answer different questions.
Tail ESS assesses the 5th and 95th percentiles; it is not an ESS specific to the
2.5th and 97.5th interval endpoints shown above.

```{r gaussian-full-diagnostics}
gaussian_parameters <- list("Random intercept" = intercept_parameters,
  "Independent slopes" = gauss_parameters, "Correlated slopes" = cor_parameters,
  Crossed = crossed_parameters, Nested = nested_parameters, By = by_parameters)
full_diagnostics <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(gaussian_parameters), function(model){
  tab <- gaussian_parameters[[model]]
  data.frame(model = model, tab[, c("parameter", "rhat", "ess_bulk", "ess_tail")])
}))
full_diagnostics <- rbind(full_diagnostics, data.frame(model = "Correlated, collapsed",
  cor_diagnostics$Collapsed))
knitr::kable(round_numeric_columns(full_diagnostics), row.names = FALSE)
gaussian_combined <- list("Random intercept" = intercept_combined,
  "Independent slopes" = gauss_combined, "Correlated slopes" = cor_combined$Separate,
  Crossed = crossed_combined, Nested = nested_combined, By = by_combined,
  "Correlated, collapsed" = cor_combined$Collapsed)
combined_diagnostics <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(gaussian_combined), function(model){
  d <- gaussian_combined[[model]]$diagnostics
  data.frame(model = model, maximum_rhat = max(d$rhat),
    minimum_bulk_ess = min(d$ess_bulk), minimum_tail_ess = min(d$ess_tail))
}))
knitr::kable(round_numeric_columns(combined_diagnostics), row.names = FALSE)
```

The largest individual-parameter R-hat is
`r round(max(full_diagnostics$rhat), 3)`; the smallest bulk ESS is
`r round(min(full_diagnostics$ess_bulk))`. These checks describe this run and
should be repeated for a new dataset or different priors. The runtime appendix
lists chain lengths and burn-in.

</details>

<details id="logistic-mixed-model">
<summary>Logistic mixed-model comparison</summary>

The logistic comparison uses Bernoulli responses with a logit link and an
independent group random intercept.

```{r simulate-logistic}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show logistic simulation code"
simulate_logistic_data <- function(seed = 1,
                                   n_group = 30,
                                   n_per_group = 12,
                                   beta = c("(Intercept)" = -0.5, x = 1),
                                   sigma_intercept = 0.5){
  set.seed(seed)

  group <- factor(rep(sprintf("g%02d", seq_len(n_group)),
                      each = n_per_group))
  x <- rnorm(n_group * n_per_group)
  alpha <- rnorm(n_group, sd = sigma_intercept)
  names(alpha) <- levels(group)
  eta <- beta[["(Intercept)"]] + beta[["x"]] * x + alpha[group]

  data.frame(
    y = rbinom(length(eta), size = 1, prob = plogis(eta)),
    x = x,
    group = group
  )
}

logit_dat <- simulate_logistic_data(seed = 1)
logit_truth <- c("(Intercept)" = -0.5, x = 1)
logit_sigma <- 0.5
```

```{r fit-logistic}
logit_st_time <- system.time({
  logit_st <- stLMM(
    y ~ x + iid(group),
    data = logit_dat,
    family = "binomial",
    priors = list(iid_1 = list(sigma_sq = ig(2, 0.5))),
    n_samples = 1000,
    chains = 3,
    verbose = FALSE
  )
})

logit_lme4_time <- system.time({
  logit_lme4 <- glmer(
    y ~ x + (1 | group),
    data = logit_dat,
    family = binomial,
    nAGQ = 1
  )
})
```

```{r logistic-tables}
logit_beta_tab <- fixed_effect_table(logit_st, logit_lme4, logit_truth, burn = 500)
logit_sd_tab <- sd_comparison(logit_st, logit_lme4, logit_sigma, burn = 500)
knitr::kable(rbind(logit_beta_tab, logit_sd_tab), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Posterior mean [95% credible interval] and lme4 estimate")
logit_diag <- diagnostic_table(logit_st,
  c("(Intercept)", "x", "iid_1_sigma_sq"), burn = 500)
knitr::kable(round_numeric_columns(logit_diag), row.names = FALSE)
```
In this simulation, the fixed-effect estimates are close across packages. The
random-intercept standard deviation is closer to the simulated truth under
`stLMM` than under `lme4`. The scatter plot below shows the same pattern in the
group departures: they are strongly associated, but the points are
not centered exactly on the 1:1 line because the estimated random-intercept
scale differs between the two fits.

```{r logistic-random-effect-plot, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=4}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show plotting code"
logit_re <- iid_random_effect_compare(logit_st, logit_lme4, burn = 500)

ggplot(logit_re, aes(lme4, stLMM)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "grey45", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, alpha = 0.85, color = stlmm_color("primary")) +
  labs(
    x = "lme4 conditional mode",
    y = "stLMM posterior mean"
  )
```

</details>

<details id="poisson-data-and-the-nb-approximation">
<summary>Poisson data with a negative-binomial approximation</summary>

`stLMM` does not currently fit a native Poisson likelihood. The package can fit
a negative-binomial model with large fixed size, where

$$
\operatorname{var}(y_i) = \mu_i + \frac{\mu_i^2}{r},
$$

and this approaches the Poisson variance as the size $r$ becomes large. We use
`size = 100` for this example's small conditional means. The extra variance
relative to a Poisson model is $\mu_i/r$, so the appropriate size depends on
the range of means, not just the observed counts. Increasing size brings the
likelihood closer to Poisson, but can also require more iterations of the
Pólya-Gamma sampler. We assess the approximation below using the conditional
means from the Poisson fit; this remains an approximate likelihood comparison.

```{r simulate-poisson}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Poisson simulation code"
simulate_poisson_data <- function(seed = 1,
                                  n_group = 30,
                                  n_per_group = 12,
                                  beta = c("(Intercept)" = 0.5, x = 0.5),
                                  sigma_intercept = 0.5){
  set.seed(seed)

  group <- factor(rep(sprintf("g%02d", seq_len(n_group)),
                      each = n_per_group))
  x <- rnorm(n_group * n_per_group)
  alpha <- rnorm(n_group, sd = sigma_intercept)
  names(alpha) <- levels(group)
  eta <- beta[["(Intercept)"]] + beta[["x"]] * x + alpha[group]

  data.frame(
    y = rpois(length(eta), lambda = exp(eta)),
    x = x,
    group = group
  )
}

poisson_dat <- simulate_poisson_data(seed = 1)
poisson_truth <- c("(Intercept)" = 0.5, x = 0.5)
poisson_sigma <- 0.5
poisson_approx_size <- 100
```

```{r fit-poisson}
poisson_st_time <- system.time({
  poisson_st <- stLMM(
    y ~ x + iid(group),
    data = poisson_dat,
    family = "negative_binomial",
    size = poisson_approx_size,
    priors = list(iid_1 = list(sigma_sq = ig(2, 0.5))),
    n_samples = 5000,
    chains = 3,
    verbose = FALSE
  )
})

poisson_lme4_time <- system.time({
  poisson_lme4 <- glmer(
    y ~ x + (1 | group),
    data = poisson_dat,
    family = poisson
  )
})
```

```{r poisson-approximation-scale}
poisson_mean_quantiles <- quantile(fitted(poisson_lme4), c(0.5, 0.95, 1))
approximation_table <- data.frame(
  percentile = c("Median", "95th percentile", "Maximum"),
  conditional_mean = unname(poisson_mean_quantiles),
  extra_variance_percent = 100 * unname(poisson_mean_quantiles) /
    poisson_approx_size
)
knitr::kable(round_numeric_columns(approximation_table), row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Extra NB variance relative to Poisson at the fitted conditional means")
```

Here the additional variance is modest on the fitted mean scale. This table
helps interpret the comparison; it is not a universal choice of size or a
bound over all posterior draws. For a different dataset, assess its mean range
and the sensitivity of the quantities of interest to the approximation.

```{r poisson-tables}
poisson_beta_tab <- fixed_effect_table(poisson_st, poisson_lme4, poisson_truth,
                                       burn = 2500)
poisson_sd_tab <- sd_comparison(poisson_st, poisson_lme4, poisson_sigma, burn = 2500)
knitr::kable(rbind(poisson_beta_tab, poisson_sd_tab), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Posterior mean [95% credible interval] and lme4 estimate")
poisson_diag <- diagnostic_table(poisson_st,
  c("(Intercept)", "x", "iid_1_sigma_sq"), burn = 2500)
knitr::kable(round_numeric_columns(poisson_diag), row.names = FALSE)
```

The combined-coefficient interpretation and diagnostic checks are the same as
in the Gaussian lesson, now on the log-mean scale. For example:

```{r poisson-combined-summary}
poisson_combined <- summary(
  poisson_st, type = "combined", coefficients = "(Intercept)",
  terms = "iid_1", burn = 2500, diagnostic_method = "rank"
)
```

```{r poisson-all-group-diagnostics}
group_diagnostics <- poisson_combined$diagnostics
knitr::kable(round_numeric_columns(data.frame(
  groups = nrow(group_diagnostics),
  maximum_rhat = max(group_diagnostics$rhat),
  minimum_bulk_ess = min(group_diagnostics$ess_bulk),
  minimum_tail_ess = min(group_diagnostics$ess_tail)
)), caption = "Diagnostic overview for all combined group intercepts")
```

The short Poisson comparison has some R-hat values above 1.01 and is
illustrative; longer chains are needed for precise marginal summaries. The
fixed-intercept and combined diagnostics refer to different quantities, so
check both when they matter for the analysis. The NB approximation and the
native Poisson likelihood are also different models.

```{r poisson-random-effect-plot, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=4}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show plotting code"
poisson_re <- iid_random_effect_compare(poisson_st, poisson_lme4, burn = 2500)

ggplot(poisson_re, aes(lme4, stLMM)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "grey45", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, alpha = 0.85, color = stlmm_color("primary")) +
  labs(
    x = "lme4 conditional mode",
    y = "stLMM posterior mean"
  )
```

</details>

<details id="negative-binomial-mixed-model">
<summary>Negative-binomial model with estimated size</summary>

This example simulates negative-binomial counts with size 3 and estimates size
in both packages. The `stLMM` fit omits `size` and supplies
`priors$size = gamma_dist(2, 0.5)`, a Gamma prior with shape 2, rate 0.5, and
mean 4. These values are an illustrative proper prior, not an automatic default.
`lme4::glmer.nb()` estimates size by likelihood methods.

The model has repeated observations within each group. This helps distinguish
observation-level overdispersion from group variation. `stLMM` issues one
warning when size and random effects are estimated together; inspect diagnostics
and prior sensitivity rather than assuming that both variance components are
well determined. Supplying `size = nb_size` would instead fit the known-size
model without estimating size.

```{r simulate-nb}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show negative-binomial simulation code"
simulate_nb_data <- function(seed = 1,
                             n_group = 40,
                             n_per_group = 12,
                             beta = c("(Intercept)" = 0.5, x = 0.5),
                             sigma_intercept = 0.5,
                             size = 3){
  set.seed(seed)

  group <- factor(rep(sprintf("g%02d", seq_len(n_group)),
                      each = n_per_group))
  x <- rnorm(n_group * n_per_group)
  alpha <- rnorm(n_group, sd = sigma_intercept)
  names(alpha) <- levels(group)
  eta <- beta[["(Intercept)"]] + beta[["x"]] * x + alpha[group]

  data.frame(
    y = rnbinom(length(eta), size = size, mu = exp(eta)),
    x = x,
    group = group
  )
}

nb_size <- 3
nb_dat <- simulate_nb_data(seed = 1, size = nb_size)
nb_truth <- c("(Intercept)" = 0.5, x = 0.5)
nb_sigma <- 0.5
```

```{r fit-nb}
#| warning: true
nb_st_time <- system.time({
  nb_st <- stLMM(
    y ~ x + iid(group),
    data = nb_dat,
    family = "negative_binomial",
    priors = list(
      size = gamma_dist(shape = 2, rate = 0.5),
      iid_1 = list(sigma_sq = ig(2, 0.5))
    ),
    starting = list(size = c(1, 3, 10)),
    n_samples = 3000,
    chains = 3,
    verbose = FALSE
  )
})

nb_lme4_time <- system.time({
  nb_lme4 <- glmer.nb(
    y ~ x + (1 | group),
    data = nb_dat
  )
})

nb_lme4_size <- getME(nb_lme4, "glmer.nb.theta")
```

```{r nb-tables}
nb_beta_tab <- fixed_effect_table(nb_st, nb_lme4, nb_truth, burn = 500)
nb_sd_tab <- sd_comparison(nb_st, nb_lme4, nb_sigma, burn = 500)
nb_size_draws <- as_samples(nb_st, burn = 500)$size
nb_size_tab <- data.frame(Quantity = "Negative-binomial size", Simulated = nb_size,
  stLMM = format_interval(mean(nb_size_draws), quantile(nb_size_draws, 0.025),
                          quantile(nb_size_draws, 0.975)),
  lme4 = round(nb_lme4_size, 3))
knitr::kable(rbind(nb_beta_tab, nb_sd_tab, nb_size_tab), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Posterior mean [95% credible interval] and lme4 estimate")
nb_diag <- diagnostic_table(nb_st,
  c("(Intercept)", "x", "iid_1_sigma_sq", "size"), burn = 500)
knitr::kable(round_numeric_columns(nb_diag), row.names = FALSE)
```
Size and the group standard deviation are summarized on their own scales.
Inspect their intervals together with the parameter diagnostics. Both packages fit the same NB mean/variance family;
priors, posterior averaging, and likelihood approximation can produce differences.
The comparison is not evidence that size is identifiable in every grouped model.

```{r nb-random-effect-plot, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=4}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show plotting code"
nb_re <- iid_random_effect_compare(nb_st, nb_lme4, burn = 500)

ggplot(nb_re, aes(lme4, stLMM)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "grey45", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, alpha = 0.85, color = stlmm_color("primary")) +
  labs(
    x = "lme4 conditional mode",
    y = "stLMM posterior mean"
  )
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Complete runtime and run-length table</summary>

The runtime table records elapsed time for the paired `stLMM` and `lme4` fits,
including preparation and warmup in `stLMM`. The `stLMM` entries here use separate
IID sampling; both strategies are timed in the correlated-coefficient section. Posterior simulation and likelihood or REML
fitting are different computational targets.
Simulation, plotting, and construction of the `lme4` indicator columns are
outside these fit timers.

```{r runtime-table}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show runtime table code"
runtime_labels <- c("Random intercept", "Independent intercept and slope",
  "Correlated intercept and slope", "Crossed groups", "Nested groups",
  "Parent-specific plot variances", "Logistic", "Poisson approximation",
  "Negative binomial")
runtime_st <- list(intercept_st_time, gauss_st_time, gauss_cor_st_time,
  crossed_st_time, nested_st_time, by_st_time, logit_st_time,
  poisson_st_time, nb_st_time)
runtime_lme4 <- list(intercept_lme4_time, gauss_lme4_time, gauss_cor_lme4_time,
  crossed_lme4_time, nested_lme4_time, by_lme4_time, logit_lme4_time,
  poisson_lme4_time, nb_lme4_time)
runtime_draws <- c(16000, 16000, 8000, 40000, 60000, 160000, 1000, 5000, 3000)
runtime_burn <- c(gaussian_burn, gaussian_burn, cor_burn, rep(gaussian_burn, 3),
                  500, 2500, 500)
runtime_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(runtime_labels), function(i)
  data.frame(example = runtime_labels[i], package = c("stLMM", "lme4"),
    task = c(paste("3 chains x", runtime_draws[i], "saved iterations"),
             if(i <= 6) "REML fit" else "GLMM likelihood fit"),
    burn_per_chain = c(runtime_burn[i], NA_integer_),
    elapsed_seconds = c(runtime_st[[i]][["elapsed"]],
                        runtime_lme4[[i]][["elapsed"]]))))

knitr::kable(round_numeric_columns(runtime_tab, 3))
```

Run times describe these particular tasks and include the different chain
lengths needed for the examples. They are not a ranking across models or an
ESS comparison with REML. The separate-versus-collapsed example
above uses equal chain lengths and includes recovery in its total time.

</details>
